ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Julius Caesar Synthetic CCD

text.paragraph: Urgent visit after a witnessed collapse with jerking and confusion, the third spell in eighteen months: history, examination, ECG, tests, cardiac monitor, seizure safety, and neurology referral. Concerns: Six days ago he collapsed at a long outdoor ceremony after a strange rising feeling, with jerking of both arms, a bitten tongue, and twenty minutes of confusion; it is his third spell in eighteen months, and he wants to know why he collapses and whether it will happen again in public; He wants to keep working, travelling, speaking, and riding; He is frustrated at being told not to drive. [S]

tr.td: 12-lead ECG: sinus rhythm at 70 per minute, PR 168 ms, QRS 92 ms, QTc 412 ms, voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy; no pre-excitation, Brugada pattern, or heart block

14-day ambulatory ECG patch, fitted the day after the first visit: sinus rhythm throughout, no atrial fibrillation or flutter, no pause longer than 2 seconds, no high-grade block; one patient-triggered event (light-headed on standing) in sinus rhythm
Routine EEG with sleep: intermittent left temporal sharp waves in drowsiness and light sleep; normal background; no seizure recorded

MRI of the brain with diffusion-weighted, susceptibility-weighted, and epilepsy-protocol sequences: no acute infarct; a chronic 1.5 cm cortical and subcortical infarct with gliosis in the left posterior temporal lobe; moderate periventricular and deep white matter hyperintensities (Fazekas grade 2); no microbleeds, mass, vascular malformation, cyst, or calcified lesion; hippocampi normal

CT angiography of the head and neck: calcified plaque at the left carotid bifurcation with less than 30 percent stenosis; no other extracranial or intracranial stenosis, dissection, aneurysm, or arteriovenous malformation
Transthoracic echocardiogram with agitated saline: ejection fraction 60 percent, mild concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, normal left atrial size, no thrombus or valve disease; no shunt
Second ambulatory ECG monitor for four more weeks (more than 40 days of monitoring in all): sinus rhythm throughout; no atrial fibrillation or flutter; rare isolated ectopic beats
Home sleep apnea test: apnea-hypopnea index 4 per hour, oxygen saturation nadir 91 percent; no sleep apnea
Advance care planning conversation, about 20 minutes

his last years; no dates recorded

6 April 46 BC in the old Roman calendar (about 7 February 46 BC, Julian)

tr.td: Work-up of transient loss of consciousness: witness account, orthostatic vital signs, 12-lead ECG today, a 14-day ambulatory ECG patch from tomorrow, blood count, electrolytes, calcium, glucose, kidney and liver tests, HbA1c, lipids, and TSH; EEG and MRI of the brain with diffusion-weighted and epilepsy-protocol sequences; CT angiography of the head and neck; transthoracic echocardiogram

Neurology consultation: is this epilepsy, syncope, or transient ischemic attack; review of the EEG, MRI, and vascular imaging; whether to start an antiseizure medicine and which; stroke prevention; and driving

Seizure safety from today: no driving until a seizure-free period set by state law and his neurologist; showers rather than baths; no swimming or riding alone; no climbing to heights; regular sleep of at least seven hours; a written seizure action plan for his staff, including when to call emergency services
Blood pressure: lisinopril 10 mg daily from today; home blood pressure log twice daily; potassium and creatinine in two weeks; target below 130/80 mmHg
Antiseizure medicine: levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily, with teaching about irritability, low mood, and drowsiness; a seizure diary; no missed doses

Secondary stroke prevention for the cortical infarct: aspirin 81 mg daily, atorvastatin 80 mg at bedtime with a lipid panel at 4 to 12 weeks (LDL target below 70 mg/dL), blood pressure below 130/80 mmHg with a second drug if needed, a home sleep apnea test, and a further four weeks of ambulatory rhythm monitoring (more than 30 days in all) for occult atrial fibrillation
Lifestyle: Mediterranean-style diet with sodium below 2.3 g a day; aerobic activity at least 150 minutes a week; alcohol kept at his present low level; no tobacco
Mood and cognition after the diagnosis: PHQ-9 four weeks after starting levetiracetam and then periodically; MoCA in the first months after the infarct was found

Adult prevention plan: influenza, pneumococcal, and recombinant zoster vaccines; hepatitis C, hepatitis B, and HIV screening; colonoscopy for colorectal cancer screening; eye examination; PSA discussion at 55
Cause of the spells established and explained to him by the neurology visit
Focal epilepsy with a structural vascular cause, from a chronic left temporal cortical infarct; syncope and transient ischemic attack judged unlikely
No seizures on levetiracetam through the ten-week review
No seizure or spell since levetiracetam was started ten weeks ago
